one_line: A feature tour of Cursor's hidden productivity tools: global and project rules, notepads, indexed docs, MCP servers (Docker example), and YOLO mode for auto-running tools.
summary: The video walks through Cursor features that the speaker says most users miss, rated on a self-assigned 5-to-10 productivity scale. It starts with Rules for AI (global behaviour preferences) and then moves to project rules, which replace the old .cursorrules file and are stored as .mdc files with a description and file globs that control when they load. Notepads are reusable prompt snippets that the user attaches manually in Composer. Docs support covers @web lookups, Cursor's pre-indexed doc list, and indexing a custom documentation URL. The main segment sets up a Docker MCP server launched with uvx, runs a tool call from Agent mode, and ends with YOLO mode, which auto-runs tools either by description or by a command allow/deny list. The content is practical but shallow; it is mostly UI click-paths with little evidence beyond one hello-world container demo.

key_ideas.idea: Global Rules for AI are for general behaviour; project rules are the better tool
key_ideas.detail: Rules for AI in settings apply to every project and suit style preferences such as terse answers, code over prose, and treating the user as an expert. Project rules are per-codebase and the speaker calls them the replacement for the .cursorrules file, which he says is deprecated.

key_ideas.idea: A rule's description and globs decide when it loads
key_ideas.detail: The description lets the AI decide when to pull in a rule (e.g. whenever Postgres comes up). Globs load a rule whenever a matching file is in play, such as *.sql, or separate front-end and back-end folders in a monorepo.

key_ideas.idea: Rules are plain files in the repo and can be shared
key_ideas.detail: Each rule is saved as a Markdown-based .mdc file in a .cursor/rules folder. Committing that folder to Git shares the rules with the whole team.

key_ideas.idea: Notepads are reusable prompt snippets that must be attached manually
key_ideas.detail: A notepad can hold a boilerplate prompt and can reference files, such as 'add a new page, use index.tsx as a reference'. It is pulled into Composer by hand, unlike rules, which can load automatically.

key_ideas.idea: Docs can be indexed from a single URL and then referenced by name
key_ideas.detail: The @web mention searches or fetches a URL for current information, such as the latest Tailwind version. Cursor also has a list of pre-indexed docs under 'add docs', and any docs site can be indexed by pasting its URL. Once indexed, the docs are referenced in Composer with @ and cited as sources.

key_ideas.idea: MCP is the highest-leverage feature, and setup is one command plus a tool list
key_ideas.detail: MCP is presented as an open standard from Anthropic that also works in the Claude desktop app. A server is added in Cursor settings under Features > MCP Servers by giving a name, a command-type transport and a command such as uvx docker-mcp. Once connected, the tools appear with a green icon, and calls in Agent mode show their arguments and the logs returned, which feed back into context.

key_ideas.idea: YOLO mode trades confirmation prompts for risk, with optional guardrails
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says YOLO mode lets Composer run tools and commands without confirmation, which he calls unsafe. It has two guardrail options: a natural-language description of which commands may run automatically, or an explicit allow list and deny list.

techniques.name: Global behaviour rules
techniques.how: Open Cursor Settings > General > Rules for AI and write terse, general instructions (e.g. skip high-level explanations, show actual code for fixes, be casual, treat me as an expert, be accurate and thorough). These apply to every project.
techniques.when: Set once per developer to remove recurring wall-of-text answers and boilerplate disclaimers across all projects.

techniques.name: Scoped project rules as .mdc files
techniques.how: Settings > Rules (below Rules for AI) > add a rule. Fill in a description (when the AI should load it), a glob (which file paths trigger it), and Markdown content (naming conventions, table/column rules, code examples). Cursor writes it to .cursor/rules/<name>.mdc; commit that folder to Git so teammates get the same rules.
techniques.when: Per-repo conventions, especially in monorepos where front-end and back-end need different rules. Split one large rules file into several focused rules instead of one file that covers everything.

techniques.name: Borrowing rule sets
techniques.how: Browse examples at cursor.directory filtered by language and copy a rule. The speaker also points to Supabase's public GitHub repo of Postgres prompt rules, which come with globs filled in.
techniques.when: Starting a new rule set, e.g. for Postgres, instead of writing conventions from scratch.

techniques.name: Notepads as prompt templates
techniques.how: Settings > Notepads > add new notepad. Write a reusable prompt and reference files inside it (e.g. 'add a new page to the app, use index.tsx as a reference'). In Composer, type @ and select the notepad by name, optionally with a parameter such as the new page name.
techniques.when: Repeated scaffolding prompts, such as new pages or components, where the same long prompt would otherwise be retyped. Notepads are not auto-loaded, so the user must reference them.

techniques.name: Web and indexed-doc references in Composer
techniques.how: Type @web followed by a search query or a URL to fetch current pages. For documentation, use the 'add docs' list of pre-indexed libraries, or 'add new doc' and paste a docs URL to index it; check the indexing status in settings, then reference the docs with @<docname> in Composer.
techniques.when: When a library has changed since the model's training data (the speaker's example is a Tailwind v4 upgrade) or for internal documentation that is not in the pre-indexed list.

techniques.name: Adding an MCP server in Cursor
techniques.how: Settings > Features (scroll to the bottom) > MCP Servers > add new MCP server. Enter a name, choose the command type, and enter the command shown in the server's README, e.g. uvx with the argument docker-mcp (npx is the other common pattern). Add it, check for the green icon and the listed tools, then in Composer use Agent mode and ask for an action, such as creating a hello-world container.
techniques.when: To give the agent tools that run outside the editor, such as Docker, databases or any MCP server. Each tool call shows its arguments and output, and that output is added to context for debugging.

techniques.name: YOLO mode with allow and deny lists
techniques.how: Enable YOLO mode in Cursor settings. Either describe in plain language which commands may run automatically and let the AI decide, or set an explicit command allow list and deny list.
techniques.when: Only for trusted, sandboxed or low-risk work where repeatedly clicking Run Tool costs more time than the risk. The speaker explicitly calls it less safe, so an explicit deny list is the safer choice.

tools: docker-mcp (Docker MCP server, run with uvx)
ClickHouse (named as a target, not demonstrated)
Spotify MCP server (speaker's own modified version)

numbers.claim: Self-assigned productivity scale: Rules for AI starts at 5/10 in the intro, project rules rated 8/10, indexed docs 9/10, MCP 10/10. These are the speaker's subjective ratings with no measurements.
Title promise of 10x productivity is not measured anywhere in the video; the only evidence is one hello-world Docker container demo.

hot_takes: Title promises 10x productivity, but the video gives no measurement; the speaker's productivity scale is subjective.
The speaker says the .cursorrules file is deprecated and that project rules are 'way more powerful'. He gives no source for the deprecation within the video.
He calls MCP 'the 10 out of 10 feature that most people completely miss', yet the demo is a single container create and log read.
He calls YOLO mode unsafe but still recommends it for trusted users; the safer option is an explicit deny list.

relevance.why: Cursor's YOLO mode with per-command allow and deny lists is a simple, user-facing example of command gating, which is related to Crucible's exec-gate guardrails. The video does not go deeper than that.
relevance.action: Compare Cursor's YOLO allow/deny list UX with Crucible's exec-gate design and check that deny rules win over allow rules.

relevance.why: Scoped rule files that load either by an AI-judged description or by a file-path glob are a context-engineering pattern for per-task instructions. The video is about Cursor, not the Claude Code CLI that ProsHarness wraps.
relevance.action: Check whether ProsHarness's instruction files can be scoped by task or file pattern, so that only relevant rules load on each run.
